text: So originally, the plan was to talk more
about reinforcement learning.
But I thought since I only had one lecture to give,
I think this class would be a little bit
incomplete without saying something about multimodality,
which is so pervasive if you look at all the major models.
So this will be an overview of multimodal models.
Of course, this could be a whole class in itself,
and I'll try to do what I can in one lecture.
OK, so let's dive into multimodal models.
So far in this class, we have exclusively
focused on language models.
And language models are already pretty general.
They give you the ability to go from any piece of text
to any text.
So this could be any language, code, poetry, anything you like,
even, let's say, DNA, for example.
But the world is multimodal.
You have text, you have images, audio, video.
And if you think about a North Star of where we want to be
is what people call omni model, which
is ability to take any combination of these modalities
and output any combination of any of these modalities.
So, for example, I can give you an image and a video
and I can ask a question about the image and the video.
I can generate images.
I can convert the audio into an image.
You can imagine all sorts of different applications
by having an omni model.
So in this class, I'm not going to build up
to a whole omni model.
But I'll give you some of the pieces that at least allow
you to ingest a little bit of images, which we'll mostly
focus on today.
So how do you build such a thing?
Well, this is a weird way to motivate this,
but the reality is that transformers work really well.
And despite the best efforts of people to try other things,
those are across all of these modalities still at scale
the best thing we have.

好，那么让我们回到过去，把时间倒回到 21 年。
所以 CLIP 模型，你们中一些人可能熟悉，
是现代视觉语言模型的许多基础。
And so we can go through this a bit in more detail.
So CLIP stands for Contrastive Language Image Pre-Training.
And a bit of historical context is around
that time GPT-3 had already happened.
GPT-2.
All the language models had already
gone into this foundation model era.
Neovision was still-- there were some efforts,
but traditionally had been based on large annotated data
sets, such as ImageNet, and training models,
such as the ResNet, on these data sets
and doing a bunch of other things, like data augmentation,
and getting really good performance.
And so the researchers at OpenAI were wondering,
is it possible to leverage the large amount of image
and textual captions out there?
So inspired by this idea in language where you could just
scrape the internet, you have all this text, it's very noisy.
But somehow if you train a large enough model,
you can make sense out of this and generate something useful.
So what was the equivalent of that for images?
So as a result, CLIP was born.
And the idea of CLIP is fairly simple and straightforward.
So the idea here is that suppose I give you
a bunch of image-text pairs.
So let's say I give you 32,000 of these.
OK, so what I'm going to do is for each image
I'm going to encode it using an image encoder, which I'll
explain later, into a vector.
So I'm going to have 32,000 of these image encodings.
I'm going to also do the same thing
with the corresponding text.
So that will give me T1 through TN.
So these are the embeddings of the text.
These are embedding of the images.
Now, the objective I want to set up
is that I want the image-- let's take I1.
So I1 is aligned with T1.
So I want this alignment, the dot product between these two
embeddings to be much larger than the dot product between I1
and all the other texts, OK.
And conversely, I also want for this text
to say that this dot product is larger
than the dot product between T1 and all the other images.
So that, in a nutshell, is the CLIP objective.
And you can imagine doing—there's basically
2 times N different softmax classification problems.
So here's the code.
So you get an n by d matrix for the image encodings
and n by d for the textual embeddings.
You normalize and you take this dot product
with some temperature.
And then you compute the cross entropy, OK.
So it's basically a multi-class classification problem,
where the examples are structured in this m by n matrix form.
OK, any questions about that?
All right, so some more details about how CLIP was built.
So where does the data come from?
There are not too many details in the paper about the data.
Roughly, you take a bunch of queries from somewhere
and then you go search online for these
and you mine a bunch of image and text pairs.
And this resulted in 400 million image-text pairs.
The data set wasn't released, but there
was an effort by this paper called
OpenCLIP, which replicated and further extended the CLIP ideas.
So there was a data set called LAION-5B,
which was released 5 billion images
with textual descriptions.
And there was a bunch of processing that happened.
Interestingly, they actually used CLIP for the data filtering
and then train OpenCLIP.
So there's some bootstrapping happening.
But at least this is a model where
you can point to the data set that it was trained
on and the code as well.
So a few other details.
So images come in all sorts of resolutions.
If you find an internet image, it
might be long and skinny or tall—sorry.
Long and skinny or the other way.
So, arbitrary dimensions.
And one thing that you learn about neural nets
is that they don't like things to be dynamic.
They want things to be fixed size.
So there is a somewhat heuristic processing
that happens is they resize the image so that the shorter side
is 336 or whatever target size.
It could be 224 as well.
And then they center crop to get a square.
OK, this is obviously for convenience.
Later, we'll see that you can do better than this.
But this is just for expediency.
And also at this time the CLIP authors
were thinking about ImageNet and classification.
So usually, the object is in the middle
and you're just trimming off some background.
So it doesn't matter too much.
So what is the vision encoder?
So this is the general algorithm.
But I haven't specified what the image and text encoders are.
Yeah.
So the question I think is why they train on image-text pairs
as opposed to images.
So there is a line of work that tries
to encode images into representations
based on data augmentation.
So, for example, if you take an image-- and I think
this idea called SimCLR.
You augment it.
You crop it.
You randomly perturb it.
Rotate it.
And you want to say that that is the same image.
They should have similar embeddings.
And that's useful for low level details.
But the problem is that you won't data
augment your way from one type of dog to another dog.
So by using the text, it gives you
a higher level semantic representations of images.
And, yeah, that's a good question.
And later, we'll see how these semantic representations are
useful if you look at the types of tasks
that people are trying to solve.
OK, so what is the vision encoder that CLIP uses?
They actually experimented with a bunch of different ones,
ResNets and vision transformers, which had just come out.
They found out that vision transformers performed the best.
So when people say CLIP, they usually mean the VIT version.
And so a vision transformer does the following.
So you take an image and you break it up into these patches.
I think the original paper was 16 by 16
and the CLIP used 14 by 14.
But anyway, you have these little patches,
which are basically vectors.
So each patch is in some sense a--
well, a token for this vision transformer.
You add the positional embeddings
just like you would if you were training a language model,
and then you just put it through a standard transformer.
And if you want to classify, then you would--
well, you would usually want to--OK, sorry.
The transformer encoder produces a sequence of vectors.
And the CLIP paper does something a little bit different.
You can average all these vectors.
That gives you a single vector.
But they thought it was better to do attention pooling, which
means that you take the global average of all the activations,
but then you also do another round of attention
with that query against the key and values of each position.
And that gives you another vector,
which is maybe a little bit more informed
rather than just a straight up average.
OK, so that's the VIT.
And the CLIP paper found that the best model is what is called
VIT-L/14.
So to decipher, this is a large VIT.
I think it has 24 layers or so.
Not quite sure about that.
And 14 by 14 patches.
Each patch is RGB, so it has three channels.
And they trained on 336 by 336 resolution images.
Actually, they trained on a lower res

And then for the latter part of training,
they train on higher res.
Yeah.
For the position embedding, would it

For example, task only has [INAUDIBLE].
Yeah, so the question is, can you

Later, we'll see a fancier positional embeddings

It's a GPT-2 style transformer since that

And in order to get a single vector out of a sequence,

And then they took EOS, the activation at the highest layer

OK, so you have the vision encoder.
You have the text encoder.
And then you can do this process to train.
You pick a batch.
You encode all the text.
You decode all the images.
And then you form these two end cross-entropy losses.
And then you go from there.

So what did we learn so far?
So we've encoded images using CLIP.
And it captures the semantics of the image
because it's paired with text.
And generally, text talks about the semantics.
It is important to note that the design decisions here are
based on image classification.
So it's not very fine-grained.
But yet, it's still, as we'll see, serves
as a robust starting point for everything
we're going to do later.
One technical downside of CLIP is that it does require large
batch sizes, like 30,000.
If you have a batch size of 1, clearly, it
doesn't work, or even 10, it doesn't work.
And furthermore, the softmax operation
operates over the full batch.
So it's not really very decomposable.
Whereas if you think about normal language model
training, a batch of examples, all the sequences parallelize
and you just do aggregation at the end.
So this point will be addressed by another paper from Google
that came out called SigLIP.
And so think about this as basically an improved version
of CLIP.
So it stands for Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-training.
And here, the main difference is that CLIP does
multi-class classification.
It says, I have this aligned text and image.
And I'm going to say this is positive against all
the other alternative images or against all
the alternative text.
SigLIP, in some sense, is a lot simpler.
It basically says for any given image text pair,
are they aligned or not?
So if I reference this diagram up here,
it's basically binary classification
where the diagonals are positive examples
and the off-diagonals are negative examples.
That's it.
So here's the algorithm.
You take the embeddings.
You normalize.
You take the dot product as usual.
But now you're forming the labels which are minus 1
on the off-diagonal, and diagonals you have one.
And then you do log_sigmoid.
So the objective is very simple.
Yeah, so the question is, does this

At least in the initial paper, they

You could imagine, I think you're probably thinking in general

The negative examples need to be—sometimes

But at least in the initial version,

So CLIP was trained 10 days on 256 TPUv3,

And you might think, oh, v4s actually

In terms of flops per second, they're actually not.
They're better because you can put more of them in a pod

But at this scale, it's really actually not faster.
Actually, 60% slower or something.
So the way that this is faster—and, of course,
I think CLIP probably did not try

It was just let's get this thing to work.
But the SigLIP paper showed that you can parallelize this
as follows.
So you have—basically, if you recall your systems lecture,

where each device stores a subset of the image text pairs.
However, there's interactions between the examples,
unlike in language model training, where everything just
factors.
So in the first pass, each device
just computes all the losses on whatever image text
pairs it has locally.
And then you send the text.
So basically, device 1 gets T5 through T8.
And now it's able to compute the negatives here.
And then it gets T9 through T12.
So you rotate around until you cover all the off-diagonal block
entries.
Another thing that was nice about SigLIP
is that you effectively decouple batch size from the loss.
Whereas in CLIP, the loss is tied to the batch size.
If you change the batch size, it's a different loss function.
So they were able to experiment with much smaller batch sizes
less than 16K.
And in that regime, it's much better than CLIP
because the loss function, if you
have too many, too small a batch size, it just degrades.
Whereas for smaller batch size for CLIP, you have more variance

It's the same loss.
They also say, well, you can go up to much larger batch sizes.
But that doesn't really help.
And we saw that critical batch sizes at some limit.
And 32K was essentially their critical batch size.
